Interactive Athlete Storybook · Case 2: Farid — Football

1. Meet Farid

Why does repeated sprinting feel harder?

Think before you flip

Farid performs repeated short sprints, tackles and changes of direction. Why does his speed decline when recovery is too short?

2. Inside the Body

Three ATP-resynthesis pathways

Why do repeated sprints demand several energy pathways?

When Farid accelerates, stored ATP and phosphocreatine (PCr) help regenerate ATP rapidly. As intense actions repeat, glycolysis contributes substantially, while oxidative metabolism supports the low-intensity play and recovery between bursts.

⚡ Rapid power

ATP–PCr system

Supplies ATP rapidly for a jump, short sprint or sudden change of direction. PCr stores are limited and recover between efforts, mainly through aerobic metabolism.

🔥 High-intensity effort

Anaerobic glycolysis

Uses glucose or muscle glycogen to produce ATP quickly. Its contribution becomes important when intense efforts continue or are repeatedly performed with limited rest.

🌿 Recovery & endurance

Oxidative metabolism

Uses oxygen to generate ATP from carbohydrate and fat. Essential for sustained movement, PCr resynthesis and maintaining repeated-effort ability across a match.

Key principle: All three energy pathways operate simultaneously. Their relative contributions depend on exercise intensity, duration, work-to-rest pattern and the athlete's fitness.

Key mechanism

ATP–PCr regenerates ATP rapidly during brief explosive actions. Glycolysis contributes strongly as repeated intense work continues. Oxidative metabolism supplies energy throughout the match and supports phosphocreatine recovery between efforts.

3. During a Match

High-intensity efforts and recovery

From one sprint to an entire match

Farid alternates accelerations, changes of direction, ball skills, brief recovery and lower-intensity movement. The key teaching point is rapid ATP provision during an effort and aerobic recovery between efforts.

1 · Explosive sprint

Rapid acceleration and high force production. ATP–PCr is especially important for immediate power.

2 · Extended effort

Repeated running, pressing and direction changes increase glycolytic demand and fatigue.

3 · Active recovery

Lower-intensity movement permits oxidative ATP production and gradual PCr replenishment.

4 · Next action

Incomplete recovery can reduce subsequent explosive performance. Aerobic fitness helps repeat efforts.

Muscle

High force demand

Fast motor-unit recruitment supports acceleration, jumping and sharp changes of direction.

Metabolism

Repeated efforts

Increasing glycolytic demand may raise lactate and hydrogen ion concentrations during intense activity.

Cardiorespiratory

Aerobic foundation

Oxygen delivery and oxidative capacity support movement between sprints and recovery over the match.

Think: Why might two players with similar sprint speed differ in their ability to repeat sprints late in a match?

Important distinction

Energy-system contributions overlap. A short sprint is not powered by only one system, and aerobic metabolism does not switch off during intense exercise.
